newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico bank bailout could cost 1/3 GDP - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Mexico bank bailout could cost 1/3 GDP - analyst.

text.p: The cost of Mexico's bank bailout program eventually could reach a third of the country's gross domestic product (GDP), or about $85 billion, a corporate finance analyst said on Thursday.

Andrew Balbus, of the New York-based Weston Group, told a conference on global investment management in Mexico City the Mexican government is underestimating the cost of bad loans due to the 1994-95 peso crisis.
"The cost of the bank bailout could reach a third of GDP ...we estimate that as much as half of all loans in Mexico are non-performing," Balbus said.

Since Mexico's peso crisis flared in early 1995, the government's Bank Fund for Savings Protection (Fobaproa) has acquired loans worth about $16 billion, a figure that could rise to $20 billion by year's end and continue to rise next year, Balbus said. He said the Weston Group estimates there are another $10 billion in non-performing mortgage loans, $4 billion in bad credit union loans and $4 billion in unrecoverable agricultural loans.
In addition, the Group estimates another $35 billion in bad loans outstanding from development banks, especially development bank Nafinsa.
The total tab could hit $85 billion, Balbus said.
When asked how the Weston Group had arrived at the figures, Balbus said they had used information provided to them by individual banks.

"We've got a good idea of what's going on in the banks," he said. Most banks will probably recognize the loss over a 10 to 30 year period, Balbus said. But the huge cost of the bailout will inevitably slow GDP growth going forward.
"We see no real solutions to this...without domestic credit creation from the banks, Mexico's economy could muddle along for the next five to six years," he said.
